name: needle
title: How Did Cavemen Stay Warm? (Lice Know When Clothes Began!)

lines: Scientists used lice to work out when people started wearing clothes.
Yes. Lice.
So how did cavemen stay warm?
Meet Moss. He's freezing.
Surprise one: body lice live in clothes.
Their DNA suggests they split from head lice at least eighty-three thousand years ago.
Maybe earlier.
So clothes are old.
They were likely made from animal skins and fur.
Surprise two: bone needles!
The oldest eyed needles come from Siberia.
They're about forty thousand years old, maybe more.
A tiny hole for thread, carved into bone.
Surprise three: needles may mean layers.
Some scientists even wonder about Stone Age underwear!
Surprise four: in Russia, over thirty thousand years ago, three people were buried wearing ivory beads.
More than thirteen thousand of them!
Many seem to have been sewn onto their clothes.
Making them all took thousands of hours.
And Moss? He tried sewing. He stitched his tunic to his leg.
So Stone Age people stayed warm with fur, fire and clever sewing.
